source: Chosen and written for Terra Tempora's history travel from standard references; each event links to its Wikipedia article and to searches on Britannica and World History Encyclopedia. Dates marked circa are scholarly estimates.

events.title: Göbekli Tepe is raised
events.short: Hunter-gatherers carve and raise giant T-shaped stone pillars, the oldest known monumental site.
events.summary: On a hilltop in what is now Turkey, people who did not yet farm cut stone pillars up to five metres tall, decorated with foxes, boars and vultures, and set them in rings. Building on this scale needed hundreds of people to gather and be fed.
events.legacy: It overturned the idea that farming came first and temples later: shared ritual may have helped draw people into settled life.

events.title: Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent
events.approx: The arc of the Fertile Crescent; farming began at many sites
events.short: Wheat, barley, lentils, sheep and goats are domesticated. People settle in villages.
events.summary: Over a few thousand years, communities across the arc from the Levant to the Zagros domesticated emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, peas and lentils, then sheep, goats, cattle and pigs. Harvests could be stored, villages grew, and populations rose.
events.legacy: Almost everything that followed, from cities and writing to states and armies, rests on the food surplus farming made possible.

events.title: Farming begins in New Guinea
events.place: Kuk Swamp, Wahgi Valley, Papua New Guinea
events.short: Highlanders drain wetlands to grow taro and bananas, one of the world's independent births of farming.
events.summary: Ditches and planting mounds at Kuk show people in the New Guinea highlands cultivating taro, yams and bananas some 9,000 years ago, without any contact with the farmers of Asia or the Middle East.
events.legacy: Farming was invented several times over, on different continents, and the banana people eat everywhere today was first domesticated here.

events.title: Rice is domesticated on the Yangtze
events.approx: Shangshan and other early rice sites
events.short: Villagers of the lower Yangtze begin cultivating wild rice, which slowly becomes a staple crop.
events.summary: At Shangshan and later sites, people harvested and replanted wild rice, gradually selecting plants whose grains stayed on the stalk. Paddy farming spread across southern China and later South-East Asia.
events.legacy: Rice feeds more than half of humanity today.

events.title: Çatalhöyük, a town of farmers
events.short: Thousands live in packed mud-brick houses entered through the roof, with painted walls.
events.summary: Çatalhöyük had perhaps 5,000 to 7,000 inhabitants, living in houses built wall to wall without streets, moving across the rooftops. Its walls bear some of the oldest known murals and its floors held the burials of the family dead.
events.legacy: One of the first places where so many people lived together, it shows how farming reshaped family, ritual and daily life.

events.title: Maize is domesticated in Mexico
events.short: Farmers turn teosinte, a wild grass with a few hard kernels, into maize.
events.summary: Over thousands of years of selection, the small spikes of teosinte became the large cobs of maize. Together with beans and squash, the 'three sisters', it became the basis of farming across the Americas.
events.legacy: Maize fed the Olmec, Maya, Aztec and many peoples of North America, and is now the most-grown grain on Earth.

events.title: The wheel and the plough
events.place: Mesopotamia and the steppe north of the Black Sea
events.approx: The earliest wheels appear at about the same time in Mesopotamia, the Caucasus and Central Europe
events.short: Wheeled carts and ox-drawn ploughs appear within a few centuries of each other.
events.summary: Solid wooden wheels on carts pulled by oxen appear around the middle of the fourth millennium BCE, from Mesopotamia to Central Europe. The ox-drawn plough let a farmer work far more land.
events.legacy: Transport, farming and later warfare were transformed; the wheel is still the image of invention itself.

events.title: Writing is invented in Sumer
events.short: Temple accountants in Uruk press signs into clay tablets: the birth of writing.
events.summary: What began as tokens and pictures to count grain, beer and sheep became cuneiform, wedge-shaped signs that could record language itself. Egypt developed hieroglyphs at about the same time.
events.legacy: Writing marks the end of prehistory: laws, letters, literature and science can be kept and passed on.

events.title: Egypt is united
events.place: Memphis, at the head of the Nile delta
events.short: Upper and Lower Egypt join under one king, beginning 3,000 years of pharaohs.
events.summary: Tradition credits Narmer (or Menes) with uniting the Nile valley and delta into one kingdom, with its capital at Memphis. The Narmer Palette shows him wearing both crowns.
events.legacy: One of the first territorial states, ancient Egypt lasted longer than any civilization since.

events.title: Stonehenge is begun
events.short: A circular ditch is dug on Salisbury Plain; great stones follow over the next thousand years.
events.summary: Stonehenge was built in stages: an earthwork first, then bluestones hauled some 200 km from Wales, then the great sarsen circle around 2500 BCE, aligned on the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset.
events.legacy: It shows farming communities in Europe organising enormous shared works, and still draws crowds at the solstice.

events.title: Caral, the first city of the Americas
events.short: On the Peruvian coast, the Norte Chico people build pyramids and plazas without pottery or writing.
events.summary: Caral's six large platform mounds, sunken plazas and homes housed several thousand people. Its builders grew cotton for fishing nets and traded it for fish from the coast.
events.legacy: It is as old as the pyramids of Egypt, a reminder that civilization arose independently in the Americas.

events.title: The Great Pyramid of Giza
events.short: Pharaoh Khufu's pyramid rises 146 m, the tallest building on Earth for nearly 4,000 years.
events.summary: Built of some 2.3 million blocks by a well-organised, paid and fed workforce, the pyramid was Khufu's tomb. Its precision shows the reach of the Egyptian state, its scribes and its engineers.
events.legacy: The last of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.

events.title: The cities of the Indus
events.short: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa lay out grid streets, drains and a still undeciphered script.
events.summary: The Indus Valley Civilization covered more land than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined. Its cities had planned streets, covered drains, standard weights and baked bricks of the same proportions everywhere, and traded with Mesopotamia.
events.legacy: Its urban planning and sanitation were unmatched for millennia; its script is still unread.

events.title: Sargon builds the first empire
events.approx: The city of Akkad has never been located
events.short: Sargon of Akkad conquers the Sumerian cities and rules from the Gulf to the Mediterranean.
events.summary: A cup-bearer who seized power, Sargon united the city-states of Sumer and Akkad by conquest and ruled many peoples from one court, with governors, a standing army and a common language for administration.
events.legacy: The model of an empire ruling many peoples, imitated from Babylon to Rome.

events.title: The horse is tamed
events.place: Steppe of the lower Volga and Don
events.short: Ancient DNA traces modern horses to the western steppe; within centuries they spread across Eurasia.
events.summary: Horses had long been hunted, but the lineage of all domestic horses today rose on the Pontic–Caspian steppe around 2200 BCE and spread fast, together with the spoked-wheel chariot.
events.legacy: Until engines, the horse set the speed of travel, trade, news and war across Eurasia.

events.title: Erlitou, China's first state
events.short: Palaces and bronze workshops rise near the Yellow River, often linked to the Xia dynasty.
events.summary: Erlitou had palace compounds, roads and workshops casting the first bronze ritual vessels in China. Many historians link it to the Xia, the first dynasty in Chinese tradition.
events.legacy: The start of the Chinese bronze age and of the royal court culture later dynasties built on.

events.title: The Code of Hammurabi
events.short: King Hammurabi of Babylon has 282 laws carved on stone for all to see.
events.summary: The laws cover trade, wages, family, property and injury, with punishments that depend on social rank, including the famous 'an eye for an eye'. The stele, now in the Louvre, presents the king as a just ruler chosen by the gods.
events.legacy: One of the oldest written law codes, and an early idea that laws should be public.

events.title: The Rigveda is composed
events.short: Hymns in Sanskrit to Agni, Indra and other gods are composed and passed on by memory.
events.summary: The Rigveda's 1,028 hymns were composed over centuries and transmitted orally with extraordinary accuracy long before they were written down. They are the oldest texts of the Vedic religion.
events.legacy: The root of Hinduism and of Sanskrit literature, still recited today.

events.title: The Lapita sail into the Pacific
events.short: Austronesian seafarers with decorated pottery start settling the remote islands of the Pacific.
events.summary: From the Bismarck Archipelago, Lapita people sailed outrigger canoes to Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa within a few centuries, crossing open ocean to islands no one had seen.
events.legacy: They were the ancestors of the Polynesians, whose voyages would reach Hawaii, Rapa Nui and New Zealand.

events.title: Battle of Kadesh and the first peace treaty
events.short: Egypt and the Hittites fight the largest chariot battle known, then later sign a peace treaty.
events.summary: Ramesses II and the Hittite king Muwatalli II clashed at Kadesh with thousands of chariots; both claimed victory. Sixteen years later their successors signed a treaty of peace and alliance, copies of which survive in both languages.
events.legacy: The oldest surviving peace treaty; a copy hangs at the United Nations in New York.

events.title: Chinese writing on oracle bones
events.short: Shang kings ask questions of their ancestors, carved on ox bones and turtle shells.
events.summary: Diviners at the Shang capital heated bones until they cracked and wrote the question and answer beside the cracks. Over 150,000 such pieces survive, the oldest body of Chinese writing.
events.legacy: Chinese characters today descend directly from this script, the longest continuously used writing system.

events.title: The Olmec of San Lorenzo
events.short: The Olmec carve colossal stone heads, Mesoamerica's first great art style.
events.summary: On the Gulf coast of Mexico, the Olmec built ceremonial centres, carved basalt heads up to three metres tall and spread their art and beliefs across Mesoamerica through trade.
events.legacy: Often called Mesoamerica's 'mother culture': the ball game, calendars and gods of later peoples have Olmec roots.

events.title: The Bronze Age collapse
events.short: Within decades, the Hittite, Mycenaean and Ugarit kingdoms fall; Egypt barely holds on.
events.summary: Drought, earthquakes, revolts, broken trade routes and raids by the 'Sea Peoples' brought down the connected palace kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean. Cities burned and writing vanished in Greece for centuries.
events.legacy: A warning about how connected societies can fail together; from the ruins came iron, the alphabet and the Greek city-states.

events.title: The Zhou and the Mandate of Heaven
events.short: The Zhou overthrow the Shang, claiming Heaven gave them the right to rule.
events.summary: After the Battle of Muye, the Zhou justified their conquest with the Mandate of Heaven: a ruler who governs badly loses Heaven's support and may rightly be replaced. The Zhou ruled, at least in name, for almost 800 years.
events.legacy: The Mandate of Heaven framed every change of dynasty in Chinese history.

events.title: The Phoenician alphabet
events.short: Phoenician traders use 22 letters for sounds, a script anyone can learn.
events.summary: Instead of hundreds of signs, the Phoenician alphabet used a letter for each consonant. Carried by Phoenician merchants across the Mediterranean, it was adopted by the Greeks, who added vowels.
events.legacy: Greek, Latin, Cyrillic, Hebrew and Arabic letters all descend from it.

events.title: The Bantu expansion
events.short: Farmers speaking Bantu languages start moving south and east across Africa, bringing farming and iron.
events.summary: Over some 2,500 years, Bantu-speaking farmers spread from West-Central Africa through the rainforest to East and Southern Africa, carrying crops, cattle and ironworking.
events.legacy: One of the largest migrations in history: some 350 million people speak Bantu languages today, from Swahili to Zulu.

events.title: Chavín de Huántar
events.short: A temple in the Andes draws pilgrims and spreads a shared art and religion through Peru.
events.summary: Chavín's stone temple, with its maze of galleries and carved jaguar-and-snake gods, became a pilgrimage centre whose style spread along the coast and highlands of Peru.
events.legacy: The first culture to unite much of the Andes, laying foundations later built on by the Moche, Wari and Inca.

events.title: Carthage is founded
events.short: Phoenician settlers from Tyre found Carthage, future capital of a sea-trading empire.
events.summary: According to tradition, Queen Dido founded Carthage. It grew into the leading power of the western Mediterranean, with colonies in Spain, Sicily and Sardinia, and fought Rome in three Punic Wars.
events.legacy: Its rivalry with Rome decided who would rule the Mediterranean.

events.title: The first Olympic Games
events.short: Greeks from rival cities meet at Olympia to compete in honour of Zeus, under a sacred truce.
events.summary: Held every four years for over a thousand years, the Games gathered Greek-speakers from across the Mediterranean. The list of victors from 776 BCE became a way to count the years.
events.legacy: Revived in 1896, the Olympics are the world's largest sporting event.

events.title: Rome is founded
events.short: Legend says Romulus founds Rome on the Palatine; villages on its hills grow into a city.
events.summary: The traditional date, 21 April 753 BCE, comes from later Roman writers; archaeology shows villages on the hills joining into a town around then. Rome was ruled by kings until 509 BCE, then became a republic.
events.legacy: Rome went on to shape the law, languages, roads and religion of much of the world.

events.title: Kush rules Egypt
events.short: The kings of Kush, in today's Sudan, conquer Egypt and rule it as its 25th Dynasty.
events.summary: Piye marched north from Napata and took Egypt; his successors ruled from the Nile delta to the fifth cataract and built pyramids of their own. Later, at Meroë, Kush became a great centre of ironworking.
events.legacy: A reminder that Africa's Nile civilizations were not only Egyptian; Sudan today has more pyramids than Egypt.

events.title: Cyrus founds the Persian Empire
events.short: Cyrus the Great builds the largest empire yet, from the Aegean to the Indus.
events.summary: Cyrus defeated the Medes, Lydia and Babylon, where he let the exiled Jews return home. The Achaemenid Empire ruled its many peoples through governors, royal roads and a postal service while respecting local customs.
events.legacy: A model of tolerant imperial rule, admired from ancient Greece to the founders of modern states.

events.title: Democracy in Athens
events.short: Cleisthenes' reforms let Athenian citizens vote on laws in their assembly.
events.summary: All adult male citizens could speak and vote in the assembly, and officials were chosen by lot. Women, slaves and foreigners were excluded, but the idea of rule by the people was born.
events.legacy: The word and the idea of democracy come from here.

events.title: The Buddha teaches
events.short: Siddhartha Gautama reaches enlightenment and teaches a path out of suffering.
events.summary: A prince who left his home to seek the cause of suffering, the Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path in the Ganges plain. His exact dates are debated, around the 5th century BCE.
events.legacy: Buddhism spread across Asia and has some 500 million followers today.

events.title: Confucius teaches
events.short: Confucius teaches that order comes from virtue, learning and respect within the family and state.
events.summary: A teacher and minister in the state of Lu, Confucius (551–479 BCE) taught that rulers should govern by moral example and people should honour their duties to family and community. His sayings were gathered in the Analects.
events.legacy: Confucianism shaped government, education and family life in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam for over 2,000 years.

events.title: Monte Albán and Zapotec writing
events.short: The Zapotecs level a mountaintop for their capital and carve some of the earliest writing in the Americas.
events.summary: Monte Albán ruled the Oaxaca valley for over a thousand years. Its carved stones carry Zapotec glyphs and calendar dates, among the oldest writing in Mesoamerica.
events.legacy: Zapotec is still spoken in Oaxaca today.

events.title: Nok terracottas and iron
events.short: The Nok culture smelts iron and sculpts lifelike terracotta heads.
events.summary: In central Nigeria, the Nok people were among the first in West Africa to smelt iron, and made striking terracotta figures with elaborate hairstyles.
events.legacy: The oldest known sculpture tradition of sub-Saharan Africa, ancestor of later art at Ife and Benin.

events.title: Battle of Salamis
events.short: The Greek fleet defeats the navy of Xerxes, halting the Persian invasion of Greece.
events.summary: After Thermopylae and the burning of Athens, the Greek fleet led by Themistocles lured the larger Persian fleet into narrow straits and crushed it. The next year the Persians left Greece.
events.legacy: Athens' golden age, with its theatre, philosophy and the Parthenon, followed.

events.title: Plato founds the Academy
events.short: Socrates' student Plato opens a school of philosophy; Aristotle will study there.
events.summary: Plato's Academy taught philosophy, mathematics and politics for centuries. His student Aristotle went on to write on logic, biology, ethics and politics and to tutor Alexander the Great.
events.legacy: Western philosophy and science, and the very word 'academy', grow from here.

events.title: Alexander conquers Persia
events.approx: Gaugamela, his decisive victory in 331 BCE
events.short: Alexander of Macedon defeats Persia and marches as far as the Indus.
events.summary: In eleven years Alexander took Egypt, Mesopotamia, Persia and Central Asia and reached India, founding cities named Alexandria along the way. His empire split at his death, but Greek kingdoms ruled from Egypt to Afghanistan.
events.legacy: The Hellenistic age mixed Greek, Egyptian, Persian and Indian cultures, and Greek became the common language of the eastern Mediterranean.

events.title: The Maurya Empire
events.short: Chandragupta Maurya unites most of the Indian subcontinent for the first time.
events.summary: Advised by the strategist Chanakya, Chandragupta overthrew the Nanda kings and pushed out Alexander's successors. Pataliputra became one of the largest cities in the world.
events.legacy: The first empire to unite most of South Asia.

events.title: The Library of Alexandria
events.short: The Ptolemies gather scholars and hundreds of thousands of scrolls in Alexandria.
events.summary: At the Museum and Library of Alexandria, Euclid wrote his geometry, Eratosthenes measured the Earth's circumference and Herophilus studied anatomy. Ships calling at the port had their books copied.
events.legacy: The ideal of a universal library of all knowledge, revived today online.

events.title: Ashoka turns to Buddhism
events.short: Horrified by the slaughter of the Kalinga war, Emperor Ashoka embraces Buddhism and non-violence.
events.summary: Ashoka had edicts on tolerance, care for the sick and kindness to animals carved on rocks and pillars across his empire, and sent Buddhist missions to Sri Lanka and beyond.
events.legacy: Buddhism became a world religion; Ashoka's lion capital is India's national emblem today.

events.title: Qin unifies China
events.short: Qin Shi Huang conquers the warring states and becomes the first emperor of China.
events.summary: The Qin standardised writing, weights, coins and axle widths, built roads and early sections of the Great Wall, and were buried with an army of terracotta soldiers. The dynasty fell within 15 years, but the Han kept its unified state.
events.legacy: China has been, for most of the time since, one state with one script; the word 'China' likely comes from Qin.

events.title: The Nazca lines
events.short: The Nazca draw giant figures in the desert: a hummingbird, a monkey, a spider.
events.summary: By moving dark stones off the pale ground, the Nazca made hundreds of lines and figures, some hundreds of metres long, best seen from the air, probably linked to water and ritual walking.
events.legacy: One of the world's great archaeological puzzles, and a reminder of the skill of desert farmers on Peru's coast.

events.title: The Silk Road opens
events.short: Han envoy Zhang Qian's journeys west open trade routes linking China to Persia and Rome.
events.summary: After Zhang Qian returned with news of Central Asian kingdoms and their horses, the Han expanded west and caravans began carrying silk, spices, horses, glass and ideas along routes across Eurasia.
events.legacy: Buddhism, paper, gunpowder, and also plague travelled these routes; China's 'Belt and Road' borrows its image today.

events.title: Augustus, first Roman emperor
events.short: After civil war, Octavian becomes Augustus and the Roman Republic becomes an empire.
events.summary: Augustus kept the forms of the Republic but held real power, beginning two centuries of relative peace, the Pax Romana, across an empire from Britain to Egypt.
events.legacy: Roman law, Latin and Roman roads shaped Europe; the month of August is named after him.

events.title: Jesus is crucified
events.short: Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish preacher, is crucified; his followers proclaim his resurrection.
events.summary: Jesus preached in Galilee and Judea and was executed by the Roman governor Pontius Pilate. His followers, led by apostles such as Peter and Paul, spread his teaching across the Roman world.
events.legacy: Christianity became the world's largest religion, with over two billion followers.

events.title: The Kingdom of Aksum
events.short: Aksum trades between Rome and India and raises giant stone stelae.
events.summary: From the Ethiopian highlands, Aksum controlled Red Sea trade, minted its own coins and had its own script, Ge'ez. Around 330 its king Ezana became Christian, one of the first rulers to do so.
events.legacy: Ethiopia's Orthodox Church and Ge'ez script still continue its traditions.

events.title: Teotihuacan, city of the gods
events.short: The Pyramid of the Sun rises over a planned city that will reach 100,000 people.
events.summary: Teotihuacan was laid out on a grid around the Avenue of the Dead, with apartment compounds for people from all over Mesoamerica. Its influence reached the Maya cities far to the south.
events.legacy: Centuries after it fell, the Aztecs revered its ruins as the place where the gods created the world.

events.title: Paper is perfected
events.short: Court official Cai Lun presents a cheap way to make paper from bark, hemp and rags.
events.summary: Paper existed earlier in China, but Cai Lun's process made it practical and cheap. It spread to Korea and Japan, then via the Islamic world to Europe a thousand years later.
events.legacy: Without paper there would be no printing, no books for all and no paperwork.

events.title: The Classic Maya
events.short: Maya city-states like Tikal flourish, with writing, astronomy and a calendar of great precision.
events.summary: In the Classic period, dozens of Maya kingdoms built temple pyramids, recorded their history in a full writing system and used a number system with zero to track the movements of Venus and the Sun.
events.legacy: Some six million Maya live in Mexico and Central America today, speaking some thirty Mayan languages.

events.title: Constantinople, the new Rome
events.short: Constantine, the first Christian emperor, moves Rome's capital to the Bosporus.
events.summary: Constantine legalised Christianity in 313 and rebuilt Byzantium as Constantinople. The eastern Roman Empire it ruled lasted another thousand years.
events.legacy: As Istanbul, it is still a crossroads between Europe and Asia.

events.title: The fall of the Western Roman Empire
events.short: The Germanic general Odoacer deposes the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus.
events.summary: After decades of invasions, civil wars and lost provinces, the western empire ended without a battle. Germanic kingdoms took its place, while the eastern empire carried on from Constantinople.
events.legacy: Often taken as the end of antiquity and the beginning of the European Middle Ages.
events.search: fall of the Western Roman Empire

events.title: Indian numerals and zero
events.short: Aryabhata writes his treatise during the Gupta golden age; Indian mathematicians use place-value digits and zero.
events.summary: Aryabhata calculated pi to four decimals and explained eclipses. Soon after, Brahmagupta set out the rules for calculating with zero. These numerals spread through Baghdad to Europe as 'Arabic numerals'.
events.legacy: Every number written today uses this system.

events.title: Hagia Sophia
events.short: Justinian dedicates Hagia Sophia, whose dome seems to float over the largest church in the world.
events.summary: Built in under six years, Hagia Sophia remained the largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years. It became a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1935 and a mosque again in 2020.
events.legacy: Its architecture shaped Orthodox churches and Ottoman mosques alike.

events.title: The Plague of Justinian
events.short: The first known pandemic of bubonic plague strikes the Mediterranean world.
events.summary: Arriving from Egypt, plague killed a large share of Constantinople's people and returned in waves for two centuries, weakening the Byzantine and Persian empires.
events.legacy: Genetic studies of victims confirmed the same bacterium as the later Black Death.

events.title: The Hijra and the birth of Islam
events.short: The Prophet Muhammad and his followers move from Mecca to Medina, year one of the Islamic calendar.
events.summary: In Medina, Muhammad led a growing community and returned to Mecca in 630. Within a century of his death, Islam spread from Spain to Central Asia.
events.legacy: Islam is the faith of nearly two billion people; the Islamic calendar still counts from 622.

events.title: Baghdad and the House of Wisdom
events.short: The Abbasids found Baghdad; scholars there translate and extend Greek, Persian and Indian learning.
events.summary: In the Round City and its House of Wisdom, scholars such as al-Khwarizmi wrote on algebra (from his book's title, al-jabr) and algorithms (from his name), alongside work in medicine, astronomy and optics.
events.legacy: The Islamic Golden Age preserved and advanced the sciences Europe later rediscovered.

events.title: Borobudur
events.short: Java's Sailendra kings build Borobudur, the largest Buddhist monument in the world.
events.summary: Pilgrims climb its terraces past 2,672 relief panels and 504 Buddha statues, a path from the world of desire to enlightenment.
events.legacy: A sign of the maritime kingdoms of South-East Asia linking India and China by sea.

events.title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
events.short: Pope Leo III crowns the Frankish king Charlemagne emperor on Christmas Day.
events.summary: Charlemagne ruled much of western Europe and promoted learning, copying classical texts in a clear new script. His empire was divided among his grandsons in 843.
events.legacy: Called the 'father of Europe'; France and Germany both trace their origins to his empire.

events.title: The Classic Maya collapse
events.short: One by one, the great Maya cities of the southern lowlands are abandoned.
events.summary: Drought, warfare, overpopulation and failing trust in kings combined; dated monuments stop over the 9th century. Maya life went on in the north at Chichén Itzá and in the highlands.
events.legacy: Studied today as a case of how climate stress can bring down a civilization.

events.title: The oldest dated printed book
events.short: A copy of the Diamond Sutra is printed with carved woodblocks, dated 11 May 868.
events.summary: Found sealed in a cave near Dunhuang, the scroll's dedication says it was made 'for universal free distribution'. Woodblock printing made books and paper money common in Tang and Song China.
events.legacy: Printing began in East Asia six centuries before Gutenberg.

events.title: The baptism of Kievan Rus'
events.short: Prince Vladimir of Kyiv adopts Orthodox Christianity from Byzantium.
events.summary: Vladimir's choice tied the Rus' to Constantinople's Church, alphabet and art. Churches, monasteries and the Cyrillic script followed.
events.legacy: The root of Orthodox Christianity in Ukraine, Russia and Belarus.

events.title: The Tale of Genji
events.short: Lady Murasaki, a lady-in-waiting at the Heian court, writes what is often called the first novel.
events.summary: Written in Japanese kana rather than Chinese, the Tale of Genji follows the loves and losses of a prince at court, with great psychological depth.
events.legacy: A classic of world literature and of Japanese culture.

events.title: Vikings in America
events.short: Norse sailors from Greenland camp in Newfoundland, the first Europeans in the Americas.
events.summary: Tree rings show the Norse cut wood at L'Anse aux Meadows in exactly 1021. Their stay was short, but the sagas remembered the land as Vinland.
events.legacy: The first time humans had circled the whole globe: the Americas had been reached from both east and west.

events.title: The gunpowder formula
events.short: A Song military manual gives the first known recipes for gunpowder.
events.summary: Discovered by alchemists seeking an elixir of life, gunpowder was used by the Song for fire arrows and bombs. The Song also invented movable type and used the magnetic compass at sea.
events.legacy: Gunpowder changed warfare worldwide and helped end the age of castles.

events.title: Cahokia
events.short: The largest city north of Mexico rises on the Mississippi, with an earthen pyramid 30 m high.
events.summary: At its height Cahokia had perhaps 15,000 people, a vast plaza and over a hundred mounds, centre of the Mississippian culture that spread across the American South-East.
events.legacy: At its peak it rivalled London in size.

events.title: The first university
events.short: Students in Bologna organise to study law, founding the oldest university in continuous operation.
events.summary: Students hired their teachers and studied Roman law. Paris, Oxford and others followed, with faculties, degrees and lectures. Similar institutions such as al-Qarawiyyin in Fez and al-Azhar in Cairo were already teaching.
events.legacy: The model of the university, with degrees and faculties, spread around the world.

events.title: The First Crusade
events.short: Answering the Pope's call, European knights march east and take Jerusalem.
events.summary: The crusaders took Jerusalem in 1099 with great slaughter and founded crusader states that lasted two centuries. Further crusades followed, and contacts with the Islamic world and Byzantium deepened.
events.legacy: The crusades still colour relations between the West and the Middle East.

events.title: Great Zimbabwe
events.short: Shona builders raise a stone city whose gold and ivory trade reaches China.
events.summary: Great Zimbabwe's dry-stone walls, up to 11 m high, were built without mortar. Its rulers traded gold through the Swahili coast; Chinese porcelain and Persian glass were found there.
events.legacy: The country of Zimbabwe is named after it, and its soapstone birds are on the national flag.

events.title: Angkor Wat
events.short: Khmer king Suryavarman II builds Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument on Earth.
events.summary: Built as a Hindu temple to Vishnu and later Buddhist, Angkor Wat sits in a city of perhaps 700,000 people, fed by a vast network of reservoirs and canals.
events.legacy: It is on Cambodia's flag.

events.title: The churches of Lalibela
events.short: King Lalibela has eleven churches carved down into the living rock, a 'New Jerusalem'.
events.summary: Each church was cut from a single block of volcanic rock, with doors, windows and pillars, and linked by trenches and tunnels.
events.legacy: Still in use, and one of the holiest places of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.

events.title: Polynesians settle Rapa Nui
events.short: Polynesian voyagers reach the most remote inhabited island on Earth and later carve the moai.
events.summary: Navigating by stars, swells and birds, Polynesians settled the triangle from Hawaii to New Zealand to Rapa Nui. On Rapa Nui they carved nearly a thousand moai statues.
events.legacy: Some of the greatest feats of navigation before modern instruments.

events.title: Genghis Khan and the Mongols
events.place: Source of the Onon River, Mongolia
events.short: Temüjin unites the steppe tribes as Genghis Khan; his heirs build the largest land empire ever.
events.summary: Mongol armies conquered northern China, Central Asia, Persia and Russia, at terrible cost. Under Mongol rule, trade and travel across Eurasia flowed as never before.
events.legacy: The Mongols connected East and West, and redrew the map of Asia and Eastern Europe.

events.title: Magna Carta
events.short: English barons force King John to accept that even the king is bound by law.
events.summary: The charter protected barons from illegal imprisonment and unlawful taxes. It was soon annulled, then reissued, and later read as a charter of liberties for all.
events.legacy: It inspired the US Bill of Rights and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

events.title: The Mali Empire
events.approx: The early capital's site is debated
events.short: Sundiata Keita defeats the Sosso and founds Mali, rich in West African gold.
events.summary: The Manden Charter, proclaimed at Kurukan Fuga, set out rules for the new empire. Mali controlled the gold fields and the trans-Saharan trade routes.
events.legacy: The Epic of Sundiata is still sung by griots across West Africa.

events.title: The Mongols sack Baghdad
events.short: Hulagu's army destroys the Abbasid capital and its libraries; the last caliph is killed.
events.summary: Tens of thousands died, and legend says the Tigris ran black with ink from the books thrown in it. The Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad ended after five centuries.
events.legacy: Often seen as the end of the Islamic Golden Age.

events.title: Polynesians reach Aotearoa
events.short: Canoes from East Polynesia arrive in New Zealand, the last large land mass to be settled.
events.summary: The ancestors of the Māori arrived in several voyages and adapted to a cooler land, hunting the giant moa and developing a distinct culture.
events.legacy: Māori language and culture are part of New Zealand's identity today.

events.title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage
events.short: Mali's king crosses the Sahara to Mecca with so much gold that its price falls in Cairo.
events.summary: Mansa Musa's lavish hajj put Mali on European maps. He returned with scholars and architects who helped make Timbuktu a centre of Islamic learning and books.
events.legacy: Often called the richest person who ever lived.

events.title: Tenochtitlan is founded
events.short: The Mexica found their capital on an island, where they see an eagle on a cactus.
events.summary: Tenochtitlan grew into a city of some 200,000 people with causeways, canals and floating gardens, capital of the Aztec Empire.
events.legacy: Mexico City stands on it, and the eagle on the cactus is on Mexico's flag.

events.title: The Black Death
events.short: Plague arrives in Europe by ship and kills a third or more of its people in five years.
events.summary: Carried along the trade routes from Central Asia, the plague killed tens of millions across Asia, the Middle East, North Africa and Europe. With fewer workers, wages rose and serfdom declined in the West.
events.legacy: The deadliest pandemic recorded; it reshaped economies and the word 'quarantine' dates from it.

events.title: The treasure voyages of Zheng He
events.short: Admiral Zheng He leads Ming fleets of hundreds of ships to India, Arabia and East Africa.
events.summary: Seven voyages carried tens of thousands of men and brought back envoys and a giraffe from Africa. Then the Ming stopped them and turned inward.
events.legacy: A famous 'what if': China had the ships to explore the world before Europe did.

events.title: The Inca Empire
events.short: Pachacuti turns the kingdom of Cusco into the largest empire of the Americas.
events.summary: The Inca ruled some ten million people along the Andes, linked by 40,000 km of roads, rope bridges and relay runners, and kept records on knotted cords, the quipu. Machu Picchu was built for Pachacuti.
events.legacy: Quechua, the Inca language, is still spoken by about eight million people.

events.title: King Sejong creates Hangul
events.short: Korea's King Sejong invents a simple alphabet so that ordinary people can read and write.
events.summary: Its letters are shaped after the positions of the mouth when making each sound. Scholars resisted it, but it slowly spread and became Korea's national script in the 20th century.
events.legacy: Korea has one of the highest literacy rates in the world; Hangul Day is a national holiday.

events.title: Gutenberg's printing press
events.short: Johannes Gutenberg combines metal type, oil ink and a press to print books fast and cheap.
events.summary: His Bible appeared around 1455. Within fifty years, printers across Europe had produced millions of books, spreading news, scholarship and new religious ideas.
events.legacy: The printing revolution made the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution and mass literacy possible.

events.title: The fall of Constantinople
events.short: Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II takes Constantinople with giant cannons, ending the Byzantine Empire.
events.summary: After a 53-day siege, the city fell and became the Ottoman capital. Greek scholars fled to Italy with their manuscripts.
events.legacy: It ended the last remnant of the Roman Empire and pushed Europeans to seek sea routes to Asia.

events.title: Columbus crosses the Atlantic
events.approx: The exact landfall island is debated
events.short: Seeking Asia, Columbus reaches the Caribbean, linking Europe and the Americas for good.
events.summary: The voyage began the 'Columbian exchange' of crops, animals and people: maize, potatoes and tomatoes to the world; horses, wheat and devastating diseases to the Americas, where most of the Indigenous population died.
events.legacy: The world's continents became connected; the modern global economy begins here.

events.title: Vasco da Gama reaches India
events.short: Sailing around Africa, the Portuguese open a sea route from Europe to the Indian Ocean.
events.summary: Guided across the Indian Ocean by a local pilot from Malindi, da Gama reached Calicut, a hub of the spice trade. Portugal soon built a chain of fortified ports from Mozambique to Macau.
events.legacy: The start of European sea empires in Asia.

events.title: The High Renaissance
events.short: Leonardo paints the Mona Lisa and Michelangelo carves David: the Renaissance at its height.
events.summary: Rediscovering ancient Greece and Rome, artists and thinkers in Italian cities put human beings and nature at the centre, with perspective, anatomy and a new interest in the individual.
events.legacy: Its art fills the world's museums, and its humanism shaped modern education.

events.title: The Protestant Reformation
events.short: Martin Luther challenges the Church with his 95 Theses, spread far and wide by print.
events.summary: Luther's protest against the sale of indulgences split Western Christianity. Wars of religion followed, but so did Bibles in everyday languages and new ideas about conscience.
events.legacy: Protestant churches now count some 900 million members.

events.title: The Atlantic slave trade
events.approx: Elmina Castle, one of many slave-trading forts on the West African coast
events.short: The first direct slave voyages from Africa to the Americas begin; some 12.5 million people will be shipped.
events.summary: Over three centuries, European traders bought enslaved Africans on the coast and shipped them across the Atlantic to work on plantations in Brazil, the Caribbean and North America. Some two million died on the crossing.
events.legacy: Its consequences shape Africa, the Americas and Europe today, from the African diaspora to inequality and racism.

events.title: The fall of Tenochtitlan
events.short: Cortés and his Indigenous allies besiege and destroy the Aztec capital, weakened by smallpox.
events.summary: Tens of thousands of Tlaxcalans and other enemies of the Aztecs fought beside a few hundred Spaniards. Smallpox had already killed much of the city. New Spain was built on its ruins.
events.legacy: The beginning of colonial Mexico and the mixing of peoples and cultures that shaped Latin America.

events.title: First voyage around the world
events.short: Magellan's expedition sails west and, under Elcano, returns after circling the globe.
events.summary: Of five ships and about 270 men, one ship and 18 men returned. Magellan was killed in the Philippines. The voyage revealed the true size of the Pacific.
events.legacy: It proved the Earth could be sailed around and how large it truly is.

events.title: Babur founds the Mughal Empire
events.short: Babur's guns and cavalry defeat the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat.
events.summary: The Mughals went on to rule most of the subcontinent. Under Akbar they were known for religious tolerance and a brilliant blend of Persian and Indian culture.
events.legacy: Mughal architecture, cuisine, painting and the Urdu language are part of South Asia's heritage.

events.title: The Spanish conquest of the Inca
events.short: Pizarro captures the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca, after a civil war and epidemics.
events.summary: Atahualpa paid a room full of gold and silver as ransom and was executed anyway. Resistance continued until 1572, but the Andes became part of Spain's empire.
events.legacy: Andean silver soon flowed around the world.
events.search: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire

events.title: Copernicus moves the Earth
events.short: Copernicus publishes his book placing the Sun, not the Earth, at the centre.
events.summary: Published as he lay dying, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres began the Scientific Revolution, carried on by Galileo, Kepler and Newton.
events.legacy: A 'Copernican revolution' now means any complete change of perspective.

events.title: Manila and the first global trade
events.short: Spain founds Manila; galleons now link the Americas and China across the Pacific.
events.summary: Silver mined at Potosí and in Mexico crossed the Pacific to Manila to buy Chinese silk and porcelain. For the first time, trade circled the whole world.
events.legacy: Often called the birth of globalisation.

events.title: The Tokugawa shogunate
events.short: Tokugawa Ieyasu unites Japan and rules from Edo, starting 250 years of peace.
events.summary: The shoguns kept the daimyo in check, restricted foreign contact and let Edo grow into one of the largest cities in the world, with a lively culture of kabuki and woodblock prints.
events.legacy: Edo became Tokyo.

events.title: The Taj Mahal
events.short: Mughal emperor Shah Jahan builds a white marble tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
events.summary: Some 20,000 workers from across the empire and beyond built the tomb, its gardens and mosque over two decades.
events.legacy: A symbol of India and one of the most visited buildings in the world.

events.title: The Qing take Beijing
events.short: The Manchus take Beijing and found the Qing, China's last imperial dynasty.
events.summary: The Qing doubled China's territory, adding Tibet, Xinjiang, Mongolia and Taiwan, and China's population grew to some 400 million.
events.legacy: Modern China's borders largely follow those of the Qing.

events.title: The Peace of Westphalia
events.short: Treaties end the Thirty Years' War and recognise each state's sovereignty over its own land.
events.summary: After a war that killed millions in Central Europe, the treaties let each ruler choose their state's religion and set out a system of equal, independent states.
events.legacy: The idea of the sovereign state behind today's international law.

events.title: Newton's Principia
events.short: Isaac Newton sets out the laws of motion and universal gravitation.
events.summary: The same laws explain an apple falling and the Moon orbiting. The Principia showed that nature could be described by mathematics.
events.legacy: It underpins engineering and space flight to this day.

events.title: Battle of Plassey
events.short: The East India Company defeats the Nawab of Bengal, beginning British rule in India.
events.summary: Through bribery and a brief battle, Robert Clive won control of Bengal's riches. Within a century, the Company ruled most of India.
events.legacy: The start of nearly two centuries of British rule in India.

events.title: Watt's steam engine
events.short: Boulton and Watt sell their first efficient steam engines: the Industrial Revolution gathers pace.
events.summary: Watt's separate condenser made steam engines far more efficient. Steam powered mills, mines, then railways and ships, and Britain's industry transformed the world economy.
events.legacy: The age of fossil fuels began, with its prosperity and its climate change.

events.title: American independence
events.short: Thirteen colonies declare that 'all men are created equal' and break with Britain.
events.summary: The Declaration of Independence asserted rights to 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness'. The United States won the war and in 1787 wrote a constitution, though slavery remained.
events.legacy: The first modern republic of its size, and a model for revolutions after it.

events.title: The First Fleet in Australia
events.short: British ships land convicts at Sydney Cove, beginning colonisation of a continent home to Aboriginal peoples for 60,000 years.
events.summary: The colony spread over a land whose hundreds of Aboriginal nations had the oldest living cultures on Earth. Disease, violence and dispossession followed.
events.legacy: 26 January is Australia Day for some and Invasion Day for others.

events.title: The French Revolution
events.short: Parisians storm the Bastille; the Declaration of the Rights of Man follows.
events.summary: The Revolution abolished feudal privileges and the monarchy, then fell into the Terror and war, before Napoleon spread its laws across Europe.
events.legacy: Liberty, equality and fraternity, left and right in politics, and the metric system come from it.

events.title: The Haitian Revolution
events.short: Enslaved people rise up in Saint-Domingue; led by Toussaint Louverture, they win freedom.
events.summary: The richest colony in the Caribbean became Haiti in 1804, the first country founded by formerly enslaved people, after defeating the armies of Napoleon.
events.legacy: The only successful large slave revolt in history; it inspired abolitionists everywhere.

events.title: Latin America's independence
events.approx: One of many centres of the uprisings
events.short: From Mexico to Argentina, Spain's colonies rise up; Bolívar and San Martín lead armies across the Andes.
events.summary: Within fifteen years Spain lost almost all its American empire. Brazil declared independence from Portugal in 1822.
events.legacy: Most of the nations of Latin America date from these wars.

events.title: The First Opium War
events.short: Britain goes to war to keep selling opium to China, and wins Hong Kong.
events.summary: After China destroyed British opium stocks, British gunboats forced the Treaty of Nanking: open ports, Hong Kong ceded, and the first of the 'unequal treaties'.
events.legacy: China remembers the 'century of humiliation' that followed.

events.title: On the Origin of Species
events.short: Charles Darwin explains how species evolve by natural selection.
events.summary: Building on observations from the voyage of the Beagle, Darwin argued that all life shares common ancestors and changes over generations. Alfred Russel Wallace reached the same idea independently.
events.legacy: Evolution is the foundation of modern biology and medicine.

events.title: The American Civil War
events.approx: Fought across the southern and eastern United States
events.short: The United States splits over slavery; the Union's victory frees four million enslaved people.
events.summary: About 700,000 soldiers died. Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 and the 13th Amendment in 1865 ended slavery in the United States.
events.legacy: The fight for equal rights it began continued through the civil rights movement.

events.title: The Meiji Restoration
events.short: Japan's emperor is restored to power and the country races to modernise.
events.summary: The samurai class was abolished, railways, factories and schools were built, and a modern army created. Within forty years Japan was an industrial power.
events.legacy: The first non-Western nation to industrialise.

events.title: The Suez Canal opens
events.short: A canal through the isthmus of Suez joins the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.
events.summary: Ships between Europe and Asia no longer had to sail around Africa, cutting thousands of kilometres from the journey.
events.legacy: About a tenth of world trade still passes through it.

events.title: The Scramble for Africa
events.short: European powers meet in Berlin to set rules for dividing Africa among themselves.
events.summary: No African was invited. By 1914, nearly all of Africa was ruled by European powers, its borders drawn with little regard for its peoples.
events.legacy: Many of Africa's borders today are those drawn by colonial powers.

events.title: Battle of Adwa
events.short: Emperor Menelik II's Ethiopian army defeats an Italian invasion.
events.summary: Ethiopia kept its independence, one of only two African states never colonised in the Scramble for Africa.
events.legacy: A symbol of African resistance; the colours of Ethiopia's flag were taken up by many African nations.

events.title: The first powered flight
events.short: The Wright brothers fly a powered aeroplane for 12 seconds.
events.summary: Orville and Wilbur Wright's Flyer made four flights on 17 December 1903, the longest 260 m. Within 66 years, people stood on the Moon.
events.legacy: Air travel shrank the world.

events.title: The end of imperial China
events.short: An uprising in Wuchang topples the Qing; over 2,000 years of emperors end.
events.summary: The Republic of China was proclaimed in 1912 with Sun Yat-sen as its first president, though warlords soon divided the country.
events.legacy: Both the People's Republic and Taiwan honour Sun Yat-sen as founder of modern China.

events.title: The First World War
events.approx: Where the assassination that started it took place
events.short: An assassination in Sarajevo sets off a world war that kills some 17 million people.
events.summary: Trench warfare, machine guns, gas and tanks brought slaughter on a new scale. Four empires fell: the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman.
events.legacy: The map of Europe and the Middle East was redrawn, and its unresolved quarrels led to the Second World War.

events.title: The Russian Revolution
events.short: The tsar falls; Lenin's Bolsheviks seize power and found the first communist state.
events.summary: Civil war followed, and in 1922 the Soviet Union was formed. Under Stalin it industrialised at enormous human cost.
events.legacy: Communism shaped much of the 20th century, and its rivalry with the West became the Cold War.

events.title: The 1918 influenza pandemic
events.place: First recorded at Camp Funston, Kansas
events.short: A flu pandemic infects a third of humanity and kills tens of millions.
events.summary: Spread by troop movements at the end of the war, the flu killed more people than the war itself, many of them young adults.
events.legacy: Its lessons on masks, distancing and closures were relearned in 2020.

events.title: Penicillin is discovered
events.short: Alexander Fleming notices that a mould kills bacteria in a forgotten dish.
events.summary: Developed into a drug by Florey, Chain and Heatley in the 1940s, penicillin was the first antibiotic made at scale.
events.legacy: Antibiotics have saved hundreds of millions of lives; resistance to them is a growing threat.

events.title: The Wall Street Crash
events.short: Share prices collapse in New York, triggering the Great Depression worldwide.
events.summary: Banks failed, trade shrank and unemployment soared around the world, opening the way for extremist movements in Europe.
events.legacy: It shaped modern economic policy, central banking and social safety nets.

events.title: The Second World War
events.approx: Where Germany's invasion of Poland began; the war had begun in China in 1937
events.short: Germany invades Poland; the deadliest war in history kills some 70 to 85 million people.
events.summary: Fought in Europe, Asia, Africa and the oceans, the war included the Holocaust, the murder of six million Jews and millions of others, and ended with atomic bombs on Japan.
events.legacy: It created today's world order: the United Nations, the Cold War, decolonisation and a united Europe.

events.title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
events.short: The United States drops atomic bombs on two Japanese cities; Japan surrenders.
events.summary: The bombs killed well over 100,000 people, many of them civilians, in an instant or from burns and radiation. Japan surrendered days later.
events.legacy: The nuclear age began; the bombs have never been used in war since.

events.title: The United Nations
events.short: Fifty nations sign the UN Charter to keep the peace and protect human rights.
events.summary: The UN replaced the failed League of Nations. In 1948 it adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
events.legacy: Almost every country in the world, 193, is a member today.

events.title: Indian independence and partition
events.short: India and Pakistan win independence from Britain; partition uproots some 15 million people.
events.summary: Gandhi's non-violent movement led to independence. The hasty division into Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan brought mass migration and violence that killed hundreds of thousands.
events.legacy: India became the world's largest democracy; Gandhi's methods inspired civil rights movements worldwide.

events.title: The People's Republic of China
events.short: Mao Zedong proclaims the People's Republic after the Communists win the civil war.
events.summary: The Nationalists retreated to Taiwan. Mao's campaigns, including the Great Leap Forward famine, cost tens of millions of lives.
events.legacy: China and Taiwan remain separately governed today.

events.title: Africa's independence
events.short: Ghana becomes the first sub-Saharan colony to win independence; in 1960 seventeen more follow.
events.summary: Kwame Nkrumah led Ghana to independence, and most of Africa became free of colonial rule within twenty years, some through long wars.
events.legacy: Africa's 54 nations today.

events.title: Sputnik and the space age
events.short: The Soviet Union launches Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite.
events.summary: Its radio beeps were heard around the world, starting the space race. In 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space.
events.legacy: Satellites now run navigation, weather forecasts and communications.

events.title: The Green Revolution
events.short: High-yield wheat and rice save India and Mexico from famine.
events.summary: New varieties bred by Norman Borlaug and others, with fertiliser and irrigation, doubled harvests in many countries, though with costs to soils and water.
events.legacy: It helped feed a world population that doubled since 1960.

events.title: People walk on the Moon
events.place: Launched from Kennedy Space Center, Florida
events.short: Apollo 11 lands on the Moon; Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walk on its surface.
events.summary: Some 600 million people watched on television. Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972.
events.legacy: Photos of the Earth from space changed how people see their planet.

events.title: The first Internet message
events.short: ARPANET sends its first message between UCLA and Stanford: 'lo' before it crashes.
events.summary: The network of the US defence research agency grew into the Internet, with TCP/IP from 1983.
events.legacy: Over five billion people are online today.

events.title: China opens up
events.short: Deng Xiaoping launches reforms; China opens to markets and foreign trade.
events.summary: Special economic zones such as Shenzhen, a fishing town that became a megacity, led China's growth into the world's factory.
events.legacy: Some 800 million people left extreme poverty, the largest reduction in history.

events.title: The fall of the Berlin Wall
events.short: East Germans cross the Wall; communist rule collapses across Eastern Europe.
events.summary: Germany reunited in 1990 and the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991 into fifteen countries, ending the Cold War.
events.legacy: Many former communist countries joined the European Union and NATO.

events.title: The World Wide Web
events.short: Tim Berners-Lee puts the first website online at CERN.
events.summary: Links, web addresses and browsers made the Internet easy to use. CERN made the web free for anyone in 1993.
events.legacy: You are using it now.

events.title: The end of apartheid
events.short: South Africa holds its first election open to all; Nelson Mandela becomes president.
events.summary: After decades of resistance and 27 years in prison for Mandela, apartheid was dismantled by negotiation.
events.legacy: A Truth and Reconciliation Commission became a model for healing after conflict.

events.title: The September 11 attacks
events.short: Al-Qaeda hijackers crash planes into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon.
events.summary: Nearly 3,000 people were killed. The United States and its allies went to war in Afghanistan and later Iraq.
events.legacy: The 'war on terror' reshaped security, travel and politics worldwide.

events.title: The Paris climate agreement
events.short: Nearly every nation agrees to limit global warming to well below 2 °C.
events.summary: Each country sets its own targets to cut greenhouse gas emissions, reviewed every five years.
events.legacy: Climate change, driven by the fossil fuels of the industrial age, is a defining challenge of this century.

events.title: The COVID-19 pandemic
events.short: A new coronavirus spreads worldwide; billions live under lockdowns.
events.summary: First identified in Wuhan in late 2019, COVID-19 killed millions. Vaccines were developed in under a year, some using the new mRNA technique.
events.legacy: It changed how and where many people work, and showed how connected the world has become.
